background.speaker: [target]
background.text: We've got to end our dependence on oil and coal. They're rising rapidly in price. That's why gasoline prices are going up, and it's why electricity rates are going up. But the new demand for oil and coal from these other fast-growing countries means that the only way we're going to escape the rising prices and the dependence on foreign sources is by switching to renewable sources. And now that the coal and oil have gone up so high and the engineers have brought down the cost of solar and wind and geothermal, now it's competitive. And if we make a big commitment to take all our electricity over to renewable sources, then the cost will come down more quickly, we'll have less pollution, lower cost, and a better national security guarantee.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: Don't we get a lot of our electricity from natural gas as well?

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: Well, some. Most of it comes from coal, some of it from nuclear, from hydro, some from natural gas, and some of the new units built in the last few years have come from natural gas. Natural gas is a little bit cleaner than oil and much cleaner than coal, and it's a transition fuel. But in the longer term, we really should switch to solar and geothermal and wind energy.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: Do you think clean coal is an oxymoron?

ground_truth: There's no such thing as clean coal. It's nonexistent. Theoretically, it might be possible many years from now to come up with a way to clean it as it's burned, but there's not a single demonstration project in the country. They're not doing anything to put substance to the slogan, clean coal.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: You've set a 10-year deadline. Is that realistic?

ground_truth: I think it is because there's some challenges. Think of the space program, the national highway system. There's some challenges that are really important to the future of the country that can't be done in a single year or two years. But setting a 40-year goal, nobody takes that seriously. Ten years is about the limit of what we can stay focused on and can sustain a really sizable national commitment. And an awful lot's at stake, because the scientists are telling us that we have less than ten years to begin massive reductions in global warming pollution or else this climate crisis might not be retrievable. It is retrievable and solvable if we start now on a bold program.

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: It's almost as much as the cost of the war, and it's almost as much as we would have to pay to go out and build new coal plants and new oil drilling rigs in order to get the energy that way. We're going to make investments in new energy supply. If we choose to do it with renewable energy, it will cost money, but once we build it, the fuel is free, the sunshine and the wind are here. The competition can't bid up the price. It's not going to run out. So we need to switch to a new system that doesn't pollute, that won't be disrupted by some war in the region, and that will steadily come down in price as we make a bigger commitment to it.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: Do you think the political will is there to change the way we do business so dramatically in this country?

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: I think we're getting there. I don't think it's there in the legislature. I don't think it's there in the government center. I think it's beginning to build pretty steadily among the people. People are really hurt by these high gasoline prices. And people have caught on after 35 years to the fact that simply producing more oil does not bring down the price of gasoline. Hasn't in the past, won in the future, because these new growing economies in the east and elsewhere are bidding up the price of oil. And so gasoline prices are bidding. We've got to break free of this limited supply of dirty fuels and shift over to a source of energy that's based on fuel that's free and equipment that's high technology and is steadily coming down in price.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: What about nuclear power because countries like [target country] get something like 75 to 80 percent of their power from nuclear.

ground_truth: [target country] is unique, it's a special case. We have a lot of nuclear plants in this country and I'm not anti-nuclear, I'm a little skeptical that it's going to play a much bigger role than it does now. I think it'll continue to play a role. But the problems with nuclear are it's very expensive, it takes a long time to build, and these nuclear plants only come in one size, extra large, and the utilities don't want to commit all that money for 15 years to get a plant that's rising in cost. And of course the fuel also has some problems because if it gets out to other countries that can't be trusted, it feeds the problem of proliferating nuclear weapons.
